477.title: Your mother's eyes
477.hook: We returned you to your mother so her eyes might be cooled (20:40)
477.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a lesson in trust and in God's care for mothers; the phrase qurrat 'ayn, coolness of the eye, is common in Muslim speech and in the du'a of 25:74 for spouses and children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umar hears Ta-Ha, and your line was the page changed him. Did you reread something that once changed you? What did it say this time? Day four hundred seventy-seven.

Musa is standing in a sacred valley, barefoot, having just been told he's a prophet and sent to Pharaoh. He's frightened. He asks for help: his brother Harun beside him, a tongue that speaks more easily. And God, before sending him, does something tender. He reminds Musa of his own story, from before Musa could remember anything. A baby, a box, a river. And a mother on the riverbank, watching it float away.

Pharaoh was killing the baby boys of the Children of Israel. Ta-Ha says God inspired Musa's mother: put him in a chest, and put the chest in the river. The river will throw it onto the bank, and an enemy of Mine and his will take him. Think of the instruction. To save your child, let him go, toward the very palace that wants him dead. Another surah, Al-Qasas, says her heart was left empty, and she nearly gave the secret away. Then, verse thirty-nine: I cast love on you from Me, so you'd be raised under My eye. The baby is taken into Pharaoh's house and loved there. But he won't nurse from any woman they bring. And his sister, who has been following the chest along the bank, steps forward and says, in Pickthall's words, "Shall I show you one who will nurse him?" And then, verse forty: "and We restored thee to thy mother that her eyes might be refreshed and might not sorrow." In Arabic, kay taqarra 'aynuha: so that her eye might be cooled. Coolness of the eye is an old Arabic way of saying deep joy and relief. Classical lexicographers explain it this way: tears of grief are hot, and tears of joy are cool. The Qur'an uses the phrase elsewhere too: a prayer for spouses and children who are a coolness of the eyes. So God, sending Musa to face Pharaoh, reminds him of this: you were saved, and you were brought back, and the reason given is a mother's grief. Before the miracles and the staff and the sea, there was a woman by a river, and God did not leave her crying.

segments.voice: Think of a mother: your own, a grandmother, a friend who's just had a baby, a woman who mothered you though she wasn't your mother, or one who's grieving a child. Picture her face. What is she carrying right now that you could lighten, even a little? A call. A visit. A meal. Telling her one thing she did right. If she's died, you can do something kind in her name. If you pray, you can pray for her. The bell holds the time.
Your mother's eyes. Musa was returned to his mother so that her eyes might be cooled, and she would not grieve. Today's word.
Your line: so she would not grieve. Today, bring one small comfort to a mother: a call, a kind word, a help with something heavy. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

478.title: Increase me in knowledge
478.hook: say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge (20:114)
478.howItsDone: Many Muslims say rabbi zidni 'ilma, from 20:114, before studying, teaching or exams, and it is often written in classrooms and on school walls in Muslim communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your mother's eyes: Musa returned to the riverbank mother. Your line was so she would not grieve. Did a mother get some comfort from you? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Picture a student in the front row, writing so fast to catch every word that they miss half of what's being said. Their pen is ahead of their understanding. Now picture the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, as the commentators describe him in the early years, when the angel Jibril brought a passage: repeating each word as it came, hurrying, afraid of losing a single one. Ta-Ha has a verse for that moment. It tells him to slow down, and then it gives him six words to ask for.

Verse one hundred fourteen begins with praise: exalted is God, the true King. Then: don't hurry with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is complete. Another surah, Al-Qiyamah, says the same thing more vividly: don't move your tongue to rush it; We will gather it and recite it for you. In other words, the knowledge is safe; you can breathe. And then, in Pickthall's words: "and say: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." In Arabic: rabbi zidni 'ilma. Commentators have pointed out something striking about this verse. In the whole Qur'an, it's the one place where the Prophet is told to ask for more of something. Not more wealth, not more time, not more followers. More knowledge. And the word 'ilm in the Qur'an is wide. It's knowledge of God first, but it isn't only that. It includes understanding, discernment, knowing how things work and how to live. The first word revealed to him was iqra': read, recite. Here, years later, the request is: more. A hadith in Ibn Majah and Tirmidhi preserves a prayer of his that builds on the verse: he asked God to make what he'd learned useful, to teach him what would be useful, and to increase him in knowledge. That's the balance of the verse. Don't rush; what's yours will come. But never stop asking for more. Many Muslim students say rabbi zidni 'ilma before they study, before an exam, before opening a book. Six words in English. Three in Arabic.

segments.voice: Sit, and think of something you don't know but would like to: a word in another language, how your car's engine works, the name of the tree outside your window, the meaning of a verse you've heard all your life. Choose one. Picture yourself learning it today, without rushing, the way the verse asks. If you pray, you can say rabbi zidni 'ilma, my Lord, increase me in knowledge. The bell holds the time.
Increase me in knowledge. Rabbi zidni 'ilma: the one thing the Prophet was told to ask for more of. Today's word.
Your line: rabbi zidni 'ilma. Today, learn the one new thing you chose, and take your time understanding it. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: Before sunrise and sunset
479.hook: be patient and glorify before sunrise and before sunset (20:130)
479.howItsDone: Muslims pray Fajr before sunrise and 'Asr before sunset among the five daily prayers, and many recite the morning and evening adhkar, including subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, at the two ends of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: increase me in knowledge, and your line was rabbi zidni 'ilma. What was the one new thing you learned? Day four hundred seventy-nine, our last day in Ta-Ha.

Most days have two edges. The first few minutes after you wake, before the world gets in. And the last stretch of light in the afternoon, when the shadows go long and the day starts to close. What happens at those edges tends to shape everything in between. Ta-Ha, near its end, tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who is hearing hard words from his opponents, what to do at both edges. It starts with patience.

Verse one hundred thirty, in Pickthall's words: bear with what they say, "and celebrate the praises of thy Lord ere the rising of the sun and ere the going down thereof." The verb is sabbih: glorify, say subhan Allah, God is far above every fault. It's tasbih, the same root as the opening of Al-Isra, glory to Him who carried His servant by night. Then the verse adds more times: some hours of the night, and the ends of the day. Commentators have long read the five prayers in it. Before sunrise is Fajr. Before sunset is 'Asr, the afternoon prayer. The hours of the night hold Maghrib and 'Isha. A hadith in Sahih Muslim singles out the two edges: the Prophet said that whoever prays before the rising of the sun and before its setting will not enter the Fire. And the verse ends with a reason, la'allaka tarda: so that you may be content, well pleased. That's the surprising part. The command doesn't end in duty or reward, but in contentment. The man being mocked is told: glorify at both ends of the day, and you'll find peace. Beyond the prayers, many Muslims keep morning and evening remembrances, the adhkar, short phrases said as the day opens and as it closes. One of the simplest, from a hadith in Bukhari: subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, glory to God and praise to Him. Ta-Ha opened by saying the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out. It closes by giving the day a frame of praise at both edges, so that the middle, with all its hard words, can be borne.
screen: `BEAR WITH WHAT THEY SAY.` · `SABBIH: SAY GOD IS FAR ABOVE FAULT.` · `FAJR AND 'ASR AT THE EDGES.` · `LA'ALLAKA TARDA: THAT YOU BE CONTENT.` · then, large: `GLORY AT BOTH EDGES.`

segments.voice: The practice is a tasbih at both edges of the day. Wherever you are in your day now, sit, and say it once, slowly, aloud or under your breath: subhan Allah. If you're not Muslim, you can sit with the plain meaning: glory beyond anything I can name. Then picture tomorrow's first minutes, before your phone, and this evening's last light, before dinner. Decide where you'll be for each. Say it once more, quietly, to mark the plan. The bell holds the time.
Before sunrise and sunset. Glorify God at the two edges of the day, with patience in between, so that you may be content. Today's word.
Your line: glory at both edges. This evening before sunset, and tomorrow before sunrise, say one tasbih and notice the edge of the day. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

480.title: Every living thing from water
480.hook: We made every living thing from water (21:30)
480.tomorrow: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field
480.howItsDone: Muslims make wudu with water before prayer, and many follow the Prophet's practice of saying bismillah and drinking in three sips while seated; 21:30 is often cited when teaching care for water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before sunrise and sunset, and your line was glory at both edges. Did you mark the edge of a day with a tasbih? Day four hundred eighty, and a new surah.

Turn on a tap and fill a glass. It takes three seconds and costs almost nothing, so it's easy to forget what's in your hand. A plant left without it for a week droops. A person without it for a few days dies. Every cell in you is sitting in it right now. Surah twenty-one, Al-Anbiya, the Prophets, opens a long argument about God with a short line about the stuff in that glass.

Al-Anbiya is named for the prophets; it walks through many of them in turn, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus and more. But before the prophets, it points at the world. Verse thirty, in Pickthall's words, asks: "Have not those who disbelieve known that the heavens and the earth were of one piece, then We parted them, and we made every living thing of water?" And it ends: will they not then believe? Look at the shape. A question, then a sign, then another question. The verse isn't giving a lecture. It's asking people to look at what's already in front of them. Some modern readers connect the verse with what biology says about water and life; many scholars caution against reading the Qur'an as a science textbook, since its own purpose here is a sign that leads to faith. Both are said within the tradition. What the verse plainly says is this: life comes from water, and water comes from God. Another verse, in An-Nur, says God created every animal from water: some go on their bellies, some on two legs, some on four. And in Muslim practice, water comes before prayer: wudu, the washing of hands, mouth, face, arms and feet. A hadith in Abu Dawud says people are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. Water isn't meant to be hoarded. So this one line holds three things at once: a sign of the Creator, a gift to all living things, and a trust to be shared. The glass from the tap is all three.
screen: `QUESTION, SIGN, QUESTION.` · `LIFE FROM WATER, WATER FROM GOD.` · `WUDU: WATER BEFORE PRAYER.` · `PARTNERS IN WATER.` · then, large: `EVERY LIVING THING OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one. Hold it. Notice the weight, the temperature, the light through it. Think back along its road: rain, a river or a reservoir, pipes, the tap. Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and drink in three sips, sitting down. If you'd like, try that: three slow sips. Feel each one go down. Then sit with the empty glass, and let the thanks be wordless. The bell holds the time.
Every living thing from water. A sign in the first verses of Al-Anbiya: life comes from water, and both come from God. Today's word.

481.title: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field
481.word: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field
481.hook: a flock ruins a field, and Sulayman is given the better understanding (21:78–79)
481.howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 21:78–79 when teaching that judges may differ and revise rulings, and that both the careful judge who errs and the one who is right are rewarded; teachers also use it to show respect for the young.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every living thing from water, and your line was from water, life. Did you save some water, or notice where yours comes from? Day four hundred eighty-one.

A farmer wakes up and walks out to his field, and it's gone. Not stolen. Eaten. Overnight, someone's flock of sheep wandered in and grazed it down to the dirt. A season's work, a family's food. The farmer goes to the king for justice. The king is Dawud, a prophet, famous for his wisdom. And sitting beside him is his son, Sulayman, still young. Al-Anbiya tells the case in two verses.

The Qur'an gives the bare outline: Dawud and Sulayman, judging about the field, when the people's sheep grazed it by night, and We were witness to their judgment. Then, in Pickthall's words: "And We made Solomon to understand (the case); and unto each of them We gave judgment and knowledge." The commentators, drawing on reports from companions like Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, fill in the details. Dawud ruled first: the sheep go to the owner of the field, as payment for the loss. Fair enough. Then Sulayman, some reports say he was about eleven, suggested another way. Let the farmer keep the sheep for a while and live off their milk and wool. Meanwhile, let the shepherd work the field until it grows back to what it was. Then each takes back his own. Nobody loses everything, and the harm is actually repaired. Dawud agreed, and changed his ruling. Now look closely at the second half of the verse: to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. The Qur'an doesn't shame the father. Both were wise; on this case, the younger saw further. A hadith in Bukhari tells of a judge who works hard to reach the right ruling: if he's right, he gets two rewards, and if he's wrong, still one. Another hadith in Bukhari has the two of them again: two women claim one baby, Dawud gives it to the elder, and Sulayman calls for a knife to divide it. The younger woman cries out, give it to her, and he knows she's the mother. In both stories, the younger one sees further, and in the field case, a father listens and lets his son be right.
screen: `THE SHEEP GRAZED BY NIGHT.` · `DAWUD: THE FLOCK FOR THE FIELD.` · `SULAYMAN: MILK FOR NOW, FIELD REGROWN.` · `TO EACH, JUDGMENT AND KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `THE YOUNG ONE SAW IT.`

segments.voice: Think of a problem you're working on: at home, at work, in your community. Now think of someone younger than you who knows something about it: a child, a niece, a new coworker, a student. Picture yourself asking them what they'd do, and actually listening, the way Dawud listened. What might they see that you've stopped noticing? Choose who you'll ask, and when. The bell holds the time.
Dawud and Sulayman judge a field. A father's fair ruling, a son's better one, and a father wise enough to change his mind. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the young one saw it. Today, ask a younger person's opinion on something real, and take it seriously. Day four hundred eighty-one.

482.title: Ayyub's call
482.hook: Ayyub calls, harm has touched me and You are the most merciful, and is healed (21:83–84)
482.carry: harm touched me; you are merciful
482.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayyub's words from 21:83 in times of illness or hardship, often in Arabic, as a short personal supplication alongside the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dawud and Sulayman judged a field, and your line was the young one saw it. Whose opinion did you ask that you'd usually skip? Day four hundred eighty-two.

Some prayers are long. They have openings and closings and lists. The one in today's verse has two parts, and it doesn't ask for anything. A man has lost his health and his family, and commentators add his wealth too. They say the trial went on for years, and nobody can tell you exactly how many. And when he finally speaks to God about it, he doesn't argue. He doesn't bargain. He says what happened, and he says who God is. That's all. Al-Anbiya keeps it to two verses. Today, the call of Ayyub, the man the Bible calls Job.
screen: `TWO PARTS: WHAT HAPPENED, WHO GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall gives his words this way: "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic it is short enough to hold in one breath. Massaniya ad-durr: harm has touched me. The verb massa means to touch, the lightest contact. He doesn't say harm crushed me. He says it touched me, which some commentators read as courtesy, a man choosing his words carefully even in pain. Then the second half: wa anta arhamu r-rahimin, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Notice what's missing. There is no heal me. He lays the wound next to the mercy and leaves the rest to God. And the next verse says God answered. The harm was removed, and his family was given back to him, with the like of them besides, as a mercy and a reminder. Surah Sad tells a little more: he is told to strike the ground with his foot, and there is cool water to wash in and drink. And then God calls him patient, and an excellent servant. That's the surprise. The Qur'an praises Ayyub's patience in the same story where he tells God plainly that he's hurting. So in this picture patience isn't silence. Ya'qub says something close in Surah Yusuf: he takes his grief to God and to no one else. Complaining to people can wear a person down; telling God is part of the prayer. You may have heard longer tales about Ayyub, with details of his illness and his wife. Those are stories people tell, from later collections. The Qur'an itself stays brief.
screen: `HARM HAS TOUCHED ME.` · `YOU ARE THE MOST MERCIFUL.` · `NO ASKING, JUST NAMING.` · `PATIENT, AND HONEST ABOUT THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your pain, simply. Sit, and let the breath settle. Find one thing that hurts right now. A worry, a loss, a body that aches. Don't explain it or argue with it. Give it a few plain words, the way Ayyub did. If you pray, you can say his line, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful, and stop there. If you don't, just name the hurt to yourself, kindly, and let it sit beside you. The bell holds the time.
Ayyub's call. Two parts: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Named, not argued. Today's word.
Your line: harm touched me; you are merciful. Today, when someone asks how you are, try one honest sentence instead of fine. Day four hundred eighty-two.

483.title: Zakariyya: don't leave me alone
483.hook: my Lord, don't leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors (21:89)
483.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Zakariyya's prayer from 21:89 when hoping for children, and some use it more widely when asking not to be left alone; it is said quietly, as a personal supplication.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayyub's call, and your line was harm touched me; you are merciful. Did you give someone one honest sentence instead of fine? Day four hundred eighty-three, the end of the week.

An old man is standing in a sanctuary at night. His bones are weak, he says, and his hair has gone white, the way fire spreads through dry wood. His wife has never had a child. He has served in the temple his whole life, and he has been looking after a girl named Maryam, who seems to be fed by God Himself. And watching her, something in him finally speaks. He's been quiet about it for decades. Tonight, in a voice so low Surah Maryam calls it a secret, he asks. Today, Zakariyya.
screen: `HAIR WHITE AS FIRE IN DRY WOOD.`

segments.voice: Al-Anbiya gives his prayer in one verse. Pickthall: "My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors." The Arabic is la tadharni fardan. Fard means single, one alone. So the plainest sense is, don't leave me alone. Pickthall chose childless because that's what Zakariyya meant: no son, no one to carry on the work after him. But the word underneath is lonelier than that. Then look at the second half. You are the best of inheritors. In the same breath that he asks for an heir, he admits that God inherits everything in the end anyway. He's asking, and letting go, at once. Ayyub, yesterday, named his pain and God's mercy. Zakariyya names his fear and God's lasting. And the next verse says: so We answered him, and gave him Yahya, and made his wife fit for him. The Qur'an doesn't stop at the family. It says these prophets used to hurry toward good deeds, and they called on God in longing and in fear, and they were humble before Him. In Surah Maryam, he asks for a sign that it's real, and he is told that he will not speak to people for three nights, though he is well. So the man whose prayer was a whisper gets an answer he has to carry in silence. Commentators point out where the prayer started: watching Maryam, a young girl provided for in ways no one could explain. Seeing God give to someone else is what made him brave enough to ask for himself.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for company. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice whether there's a loneliness you've stopped mentioning, even to yourself. A friend you lost touch with, a home that's too quiet, a hope you set down years ago. Or think of someone else who is alone right now. If you pray, you can use Zakariyya's words, my Lord, don't leave me alone, for yourself or for them. If you don't, just hold that person in mind for a while. The bell holds the time.
Zakariyya. The old servant of the sanctuary who asked, in secret, not to be left alone, and was given Yahya. Today's word.

Your line: don't leave me alone. Look back at this week: a mother's eyes, more knowledge, glory at both edges, life from water, a young judge, Ayyub, Zakariyya. Today, message someone who might be lonely. Day four hundred eighty-three.

what it means: he asks not to be left alone, and in the same breath calls God the best of inheritors, the one who keeps everything in the end.
what a scholar hears: fard, single, in 21:89; Surah Maryam (19:2–11) calls the call nida'an khafiyya, a hidden call, and Aal Imran 3:37–38 places it after he sees Maryam's provision.
